alabama.ag_notification_note: Only if more than 1,000 Alabama residents must be notified — then the company must also tell the Attorney General and the consumer reporting agencies within 45 days.
alabama.agency_name: Office of the Attorney General of Alabama
alabama.freeze_rights_note: Federal law lets you place a free security freeze with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion, and lift it for free when you need credit. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name, so set one up with each bureau if your information was exposed.
alabama.notification_deadline_note: Notice must go out as fast as possible and without unreasonable delay, and no later than 45 days after the company determines a breach happened that is reasonably likely to cause substantial harm. Law enforcement can ask for a delay if notice would interfere with a criminal investigation.
alabama.private_right_note: No — only the Attorney General can enforce the law, including civil penalties of up to $5,000 per day, capped at $500,000 per breach. You cannot sue under this statute.
alabama.state_note: Alabama's law is harm-based: if the company investigates and documents that harm is not reasonably likely, it may skip notifying you — but it must first send that written determination to the Attorney General.
alabama.statute_name: Alabama Data Breach Notification Act of 2018

alaska.ag_notification_note: No. Alaska does not require the company to notify the Attorney General about a breach. If more than 1,000 residents are affected, the company must notify the nationwide credit bureaus instead. The AG only gets a written notice if the company claims no harm is likely and skips notifying you.
alaska.agency_name: Alaska Department of Law, Office of the Attorney General
alaska.freeze_rights_note: Alaska's own freeze law sits in the same act, and federal law makes freezes free: you can freeze your credit file with each of the three bureaus at no cost and lift it for free when you apply for credit.
alaska.notification_deadline_note: The law sets no number of days. The company must tell you in the most expeditious time possible and without unreasonable delay, allowing time to figure out the scope of the breach and fix the system. Police can ask for a delay during a criminal investigation.
alaska.private_right_note: Limited. A violation counts as an unfair or deceptive trade practice, and you can seek your actual economic damages, capped at $500. The state can also fine the company up to $500 per resident not notified, capped at $50,000.
alaska.state_note: Alaska has no fixed deadline in days and no duty to tell the Attorney General, so if you hear nothing, check your credit reports and consider a freeze rather than waiting for an official notice.

arizona.ag_notification_note: Only if the breach requires notifying more than 1,000 people — then the company must also notify the Attorney General and the director of the Arizona Department of Homeland Security in writing, within the same 45 days.
arizona.freeze_rights_note: Federal law lets you place a free security freeze with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion, and lift it for free when you need credit. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name.
arizona.notification_deadline_note: The clock starts when the company's investigation determines a breach occurred. Notice must be made in the most expedient manner possible and without unreasonable delay, and in any case within 45 days after that determination. Law enforcement can ask for a delay during a criminal investigation.
arizona.private_right_note: No. The statute says only the Attorney General may enforce it, with civil penalties up to $500,000 per breach. You cannot sue under this statute.
arizona.state_note: Arizona is unusual in also requiring notice to the state homeland security director for big breaches, and the breach notice itself must include the toll-free numbers for the three credit bureaus and the FTC.

arkansas.ag_notification_note: Only if the breach affects the personal information of more than 1,000 individuals — then the company must tell the Attorney General at the same time it notifies you, or within 45 days after determining harm is reasonably likely, whichever comes first.
arkansas.agency_name: Office of the Arkansas Attorney General
arkansas.freeze_rights_note: Federal law lets you place a free security freeze with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion, and lift it for free when you need credit. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name.
arkansas.notification_deadline_note: Arkansas sets no number of days. The company must tell you in the most expedient time and manner possible and without unreasonable delay, allowing time to determine the scope and restore the system. No notice is needed at all if the company determines after investigation that there is no reasonable likelihood of harm.
arkansas.private_right_note: No. Violations are enforced only by the Attorney General under the Deceptive Trade Practices Act. The statute gives individuals no right to sue.
arkansas.state_note: Arkansas has no fixed number of days for notifying you, and notice can be skipped entirely if the company decides harm is not reasonably likely — so watch your accounts and credit reports yourself.

california.ag_notification_note: If more than 500 California residents must be notified from a single breach, the company must electronically send a sample copy of the notice to the Attorney General within 15 calendar days after notifying consumers. The Attorney General publishes these notices.
california.agency_name: California Department of Justice, Office of the Attorney General
california.freeze_rights_note: Federal law makes credit freezes free at all three bureaus, and California law also gives you a free freeze right. A freeze is the strongest step you can take — it stops new accounts from being opened in your name.
california.notification_deadline_note: Since January 1, 2026, notice must go out within 30 calendar days of discovery or notification of the breach, with delays allowed only for law enforcement needs or to determine the scope and restore the system. The notice must be in plain language, titled 'Notice of Data Breach,' with set headings.
california.private_right_note: Limited but real. Under the CCPA (Civil Code § 1798.150), you can sue if your unencrypted personal information was accessed and stolen or disclosed because the business failed to use reasonable security — for $100 to $750 per consumer per incident or your actual damages, whichever is greater. For statutory damages you must first give the business 30 days' written notice and a chance to cure.
california.state_note: California is the strongest of these ten states: a 30-day deadline, a sample notice to the Attorney General for breaches over 500 people, and a required offer of at least 12 months of free identity-theft prevention services if your Social Security or driver's license number was exposed and the company was the source of the breach. Note the Legal Aid Association of California is a statewide association, not a law firm — it points you to your local legal aid office.

colorado.ag_notification_note: If the breach is reasonably believed to have affected 500 or more Colorado residents, the company must also notify the Attorney General within 30 days of determining the breach occurred.
colorado.agency_name: Colorado Attorney General's Office (Colorado Department of Law)
colorado.freeze_rights_note: Federal law lets you place a free security freeze with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion, and lift it for free when you need credit. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name.
colorado.notification_deadline_note: Notice must go out in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, but no later than 30 days after the company determines a breach occurred. Law enforcement can ask for a delay during a criminal investigation.
colorado.private_right_note: No. The Attorney General enforces the law and can sue for compliance or direct economic damages. The statute creates no private right for consumers.
colorado.state_note: Colorado's 30-day deadline is one of the shortest in the country, and the breach notice must include the toll-free numbers for the credit bureaus and the FTC plus a statement about fraud alerts and security freezes.

connecticut.ag_notification_note: Yes — for every breach, with no minimum number of people. The company must notify the Attorney General no later than the time it notifies affected residents.
connecticut.agency_name: Connecticut Office of the Attorney General
connecticut.freeze_rights_note: Federal law makes credit freezes free at all three bureaus. Connecticut's breach notice must also tell you how to place a freeze on your credit file.
connecticut.notification_deadline_note: Notice must go out without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovery of the breach, unless a shorter time is required under federal law. If more affected residents turn up after 60 days, the company must still notify them as quickly as possible. No notice is needed if the company reasonably determines the breach will not likely cause harm.
connecticut.private_right_note: No. A violation is treated as an unfair trade practice, but enforcement is by the Attorney General only — the statute creates no private right for consumers.
connecticut.state_note: Connecticut is one of only three states in this set that require free identity-theft help: if your Social Security number was involved, the company must offer you at least 24 months of free identity-theft prevention and mitigation services, and the Attorney General must be told about every breach, not just big ones.
connecticut.statute_name: Breach of Security Involving Computerized Data Containing Personal Information

delaware.ag_notification_note: Only if more than 500 Delaware residents must be notified — then the company must tell the Attorney General no later than the time it notifies residents.
delaware.agency_name: Delaware Department of Justice, Office of the Attorney General
delaware.freeze_rights_note: Federal law makes credit freezes free at all three bureaus, and Delaware's own law requires the breach notice to include information on how to place a freeze on your credit file.
delaware.notification_deadline_note: Notice must be made without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after the company determines a breach occurred, unless federal law requires a shorter time or law enforcement asks for a delay. No notice is needed if the company reasonably determines the breach is unlikely to harm you.
delaware.private_right_note: No. The 2017 amendment removed the private right the original 2005 law had. Only the Attorney General can bring an action under this chapter, including to recover direct economic damages.
delaware.state_note: If your Social Security number was in the breach, Delaware requires the company to offer you one year of free credit monitoring and to explain how to freeze your credit — take them up on both.

florida.ag_notification_note: Yes — the notice goes to the Department of Legal Affairs (the Attorney General's office). Any breach affecting 500 or more Floridians must be reported to the Department within 30 days, and even a 'no harm' determination must be sent to the Department within 30 days.
florida.agency_name: Florida Attorney General, Department of Legal Affairs
florida.freeze_rights_note: Federal law lets you place a free security freeze with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion, and lift it for free when you need credit. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name.
florida.notification_deadline_note: Notice to you must go out as expeditiously as practicable and without unreasonable delay, but no later than 30 days after the company determines a breach occurred or has reason to believe one did. Law enforcement can delay notice during a criminal investigation, and the company can get 15 extra days if it shows good cause in writing to the Department.
florida.private_right_note: No. The statute says so directly: it does not establish a private cause of action. Only the Department can enforce it, with civil penalties up to $500,000 per breach.
florida.state_note: Florida has one of the tightest deadlines (30 days) and makes the company report to the state even when it claims no harm will result — if you get a breach letter, check whether the company offered any free services, because Florida does not require it to.

georgia.ag_notification_note: No. The notification statute never names the Attorney General, so a private company has no duty to tell the AG about a breach. If more than 10,000 Georgia residents must be notified at once, the company must instead notify the nationwide consumer reporting agencies.
georgia.agency_name: Georgia Department of Law, Office of the Attorney General
georgia.freeze_rights_note: Georgia has its own freeze law, and federal law makes freezes free at all three bureaus — place one if your Social Security or driver's license number was exposed.
georgia.notification_deadline_note: Georgia sets no number of days. The company must notify you in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, allowing time to determine the scope and restore the system. Law enforcement can delay notice during a criminal investigation.
georgia.private_right_note: No. The Personal Identity Protection Act gives you no right to sue under it; the Attorney General enforces violations as unfair practices under the Fair Business Practices Act. You may still have claims under other laws, such as negligence.
georgia.state_note: Georgia is the weakest timeline in this set: no deadline in days, no notice to the Attorney General, and no required credit monitoring — so act on your own fast: freeze your credit and watch your accounts yourself.

hawaii.ag_notification_note: Only if the business notifies more than 1,000 people at one time must it also notify, in writing and without unreasonable delay, the Hawaii Office of Consumer Protection (not the Attorney General directly) and the nationwide consumer reporting agencies.
hawaii.agency_name: Hawaii Office of Consumer Protection (Department of Commerce and Consumer Affairs)
hawaii.freeze_rights_note: Under federal law you can place a free security freeze on your credit file at each of the three nationwide bureaus (Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion). A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name, and you can lift or remove it for free whenever you need to apply for credit.
hawaii.notification_deadline_note: Notice must go out without unreasonable delay after discovery or notification of the breach, allowing time to find contact information, determine the scope, and restore the system. Hawaii sets no fixed number of days; law enforcement may ask for a delay in writing if notice would impede an investigation or jeopardize national security.
hawaii.private_right_note: Under HRS 487N-3, a business that violates the law is liable to the injured person for actual damages, and the court may award attorneys' fees. The Attorney General or the Office of Consumer Protection may also bring an enforcement action, with penalties up to $2,500 per violation.
hawaii.state_note: Hawaii is unusual in that breach reports go to the Office of Consumer Protection rather than the Attorney General, and only for breaches affecting more than 1,000 people. The breach notice itself must advise you to stay vigilant by reviewing account statements and checking your free credit reports.

idaho.ag_notification_note: A city, county, or state agency must notify the Idaho Attorney General within 24 hours of discovering a breach. A private business may report a breach to the Attorney General but is not required to do so.
idaho.agency_name: Idaho Office of the Attorney General, Consumer Protection Division
idaho.freeze_rights_note: Under federal law you can place a free security freeze on your credit file at each of the three nationwide bureaus (Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion). A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name, and you can lift or remove it for free whenever you need to apply for credit.
idaho.notification_deadline_note: After a good-faith, prompt investigation finds that misuse of your information has occurred or is reasonably likely to occur, notice must go out as soon as possible, in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay. Idaho sets no fixed number of days; notice may be delayed if law enforcement says it would impede a criminal investigation.
idaho.private_right_note: Under Idaho Code 28-51-107, only the breached entity's primary regulator (the Attorney General for most businesses) may bring a civil action to enforce the notice law. An intentional failure to notify can draw a fine of up to $25,000 per breach, but you cannot sue under this statute yourself.
idaho.state_note: Idaho's duty to tell you only kicks in after the investigation finds misuse happened or is reasonably likely — so a breach alone, with no likely misuse, may never trigger a notice to you. Only government agencies, not private companies, must tell the Attorney General, and they have just 24 hours to do it.
idaho.statute_name: Disclosure of Breach of Security of Computerized Personal Information

illinois.ag_notification_note: A private data collector must notify the Illinois Attorney General when a single breach requires notice to more than 500 Illinois residents, and that notice must go out no later than the notice to consumers. State agencies have a lower threshold of 250 residents and a 45-day deadline for AG notice.
illinois.agency_name: Office of the Illinois Attorney General
illinois.freeze_rights_note: Under federal law you can place a free security freeze on your credit file at each of the three nationwide bureaus (Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion). A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name, and you can lift or remove it for free whenever you need to apply for credit.
illinois.notification_deadline_note: A data collector must notify you in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay after discovering or being told of the breach. Illinois sets no fixed day count for consumer notice; delay is allowed only to determine the scope of the breach and restore the system, or on a written law-enforcement request.
illinois.private_right_note: The Personal Information Protection Act creates no standalone private lawsuit, but Section 20 makes a violation an unlawful practice under the Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act, under which consumers can sue for damages. The Attorney General also enforces the Act.
illinois.state_note: Illinois has one of the broadest breach laws in the country: it covers paper and written records as well as computerized data, and the notice to you must include toll-free numbers for the consumer reporting agencies and the Attorney General — but it must not state how many Illinois residents were affected.

indiana.ag_notification_note: Every breach that must be disclosed to Indiana residents must also be disclosed to the Indiana Attorney General — there is no minimum number of affected residents. If more than 1,000 consumers are notified, the nationwide consumer reporting agencies must also be told.
indiana.agency_name: Indiana Office of the Attorney General
indiana.freeze_rights_note: Under federal law you can place a free security freeze on your credit file at each of the three nationwide bureaus (Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion). A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name, and you can lift or remove it for free whenever you need to apply for credit.
indiana.notification_deadline_note: Notice must go out without unreasonable delay, but no more than 45 days after discovery of the breach (a hard cap added in 2022). A delay counts as reasonable only if it is needed to restore the computer system, discover the scope of the breach, or because the Attorney General or law enforcement asked for a delay.
indiana.private_right_note: Only the Attorney General can sue under the breach law. A violation is treated as a deceptive act, and the Attorney General may seek an injunction and a civil penalty of up to $150,000 per deceptive act, but you cannot sue the company yourself under this statute.
indiana.state_note: Indiana is one of the few states where the Attorney General must hear about every notifiable breach, even if only one resident is affected. Note that state agencies follow a separate law (IC 4-1-11) with no fixed deadline and no AG notice duty.

iowa.ag_notification_note: Only if a breach requires notice to more than 500 Iowa residents must the company give written notice to the director of the Consumer Protection Division of the Attorney General's office, within five business days after notifying consumers.
iowa.agency_name: Iowa Attorney General, Consumer Protection Division
iowa.freeze_rights_note: Under federal law you can place a free security freeze on your credit file at each of the three nationwide bureaus (Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion). A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name, and you can lift or remove it for free whenever you need to apply for credit.
iowa.notification_deadline_note: Notice must be made in the most expeditious manner possible and without unreasonable delay after discovery. The current Iowa Code sets no fixed number of days (a 45-day figure in some secondary sources reflects a proposed bill, not the enacted text). Time is allowed to determine contact information and the scope of the breach, and law enforcement may request a delay in writing.
iowa.private_right_note: A violation is an unlawful practice under Iowa Code 714.16, enforced by the Attorney General, who may seek damages on behalf of a person injured by the violation. There is no direct private lawsuit under Section 715C.2 itself, though other rights and remedies are preserved.
iowa.state_note: Iowa lets a company skip notice entirely if, after an appropriate investigation, it finds no reasonable likelihood of financial harm to consumers — but it must put that finding in writing and keep the documentation for five years.

kansas.ag_notification_note: Kansas law imposes no duty to notify the Attorney General after a breach. The only third-party notice required is to the nationwide consumer reporting agencies when more than 1,000 consumers must be notified at one time. The Attorney General enforces the law but does not receive breach reports under it.
kansas.agency_name: Kansas Attorney General, Consumer Protection Division
kansas.freeze_rights_note: Under federal law you can place a free security freeze on your credit file at each of the three nationwide bureaus (Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion). A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name, and you can lift or remove it for free whenever you need to apply for credit.
kansas.notification_deadline_note: After a good-faith, prompt investigation finds that misuse of your information has occurred or is reasonably likely to occur, notice must go out as soon as possible, in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay. Kansas sets no fixed number of days; notice may be delayed if law enforcement says it would impede a criminal investigation.
kansas.private_right_note: Only the Attorney General may bring an action for violations (the Insurance Commissioner alone enforces against licensed insurance companies). The statute gives you no private right to sue the breached company.
kansas.state_note: Kansas is one of the few states with no duty to tell the Attorney General at all — the AG only comes in as enforcer. If 1,000 or more people must be notified, the credit bureaus get told instead, so they can brace for a wave of freeze and fraud-alert requests.

kentucky.ag_notification_note: The private-sector breach statute (KRS 365.732) requires no notice to any state office. If more than 1,000 people must be notified at one time, the company must also notify, without unreasonable delay, all nationwide consumer reporting agencies. (Government agencies follow a separate law with a 72-hour reporting chain.)
kentucky.agency_name: Kentucky Office of the Attorney General
kentucky.freeze_rights_note: Under federal law you can place a free security freeze on your credit file at each of the three nationwide bureaus (Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion). A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name, and you can lift or remove it for free whenever you need to apply for credit.
kentucky.legal_aid_name: Kentucky Justice Online (Legal Aid Network of Kentucky)
kentucky.notification_deadline_note: Notice must be made in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay after discovery of the breach, allowing time to determine the scope and restore the system. Kentucky sets no fixed number of days; notice may be delayed if law enforcement determines it would impede a criminal investigation.
kentucky.private_right_note: KRS 365.732 contains no enforcement clause of its own and creates no private right of action. You can still file a complaint with the Attorney General under Kentucky's general consumer-protection laws, but you cannot sue the company under the breach-notification statute itself.
kentucky.state_note: Kentucky's trigger is narrower than most states: an incident only counts as a breach if it causes, or is reasonably believed to cause, identity theft or fraud against a Kentucky resident. Kentucky has four regional legal-aid programs rather than one statewide program; Kentucky Justice Online is their shared statewide site.

louisiana.ag_notification_note: The Consumer Protection Section of the Attorney General must be notified of every breach that requires notice to Louisiana residents. Notice is timely if received within 10 days of the notice going out to residents, and it must include the names of all affected Louisiana citizens; each day late counts as a separate violation.
louisiana.agency_name: Louisiana Attorney General, Consumer Protection Section
louisiana.freeze_rights_note: Under federal law you can place a free security freeze on your credit file at each of the three nationwide bureaus (Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion). A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name, and you can lift or remove it for free whenever you need to apply for credit.
louisiana.notification_deadline_note: Notice must be made in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, but no later than 60 days from discovery of the breach. If notice is delayed, the company must give the Attorney General its reasons in writing within that 60-day period, and the Attorney General may allow a reasonable extension. No notice is required if a reasonable investigation finds no reasonable likelihood of harm, documented in writing and kept for five years.
louisiana.private_right_note: Under La. Rev. Stat. 51:3075, a civil action may be brought to recover actual damages resulting from a company's failure to disclose a breach in a timely manner. The Attorney General may also bring an enforcement action.
louisiana.state_note: Louisiana is one of the few states where you can sue for actual damages if the company is late telling you about the breach — and the Attorney General must receive the names of every Louisiana resident affected, within 10 days of your notice.

maine.ag_notification_note: When notice to Maine residents is required, the company must also notify the appropriate state regulators within the Department of Professional and Financial Regulation, or the Attorney General if the company is not regulated by that department. There is no minimum number of affected residents.
maine.agency_name: Maine Office of the Attorney General
maine.freeze_rights_note: Under federal law you can place a free security freeze on your credit file at each of the three nationwide bureaus (Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion). A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name, and you can lift or remove it for free whenever you need to apply for credit.
maine.notification_deadline_note: Notice must be made as expediently as possible and without unreasonable delay, but no more than 30 days after the person becomes aware of the breach and identifies its scope. If law enforcement asks for a delay, notice must then go out within seven business days after law enforcement says it will no longer compromise the investigation.
maine.private_right_note: The Notice of Risk to Personal Data Act creates no private right of action; it is enforced by the Department of Professional and Financial Regulation for entities it regulates and by the Attorney General for everyone else. Violations carry fines up to $500 per violation, capped at $2,500 per day, plus equitable relief.
maine.state_note: Maine has one of the shortest breach deadlines in the country — 30 days from when the company both learns of the breach and figures out its scope. Information brokers and other businesses also have slightly different triggers for when notice is owed in the first place.
maine.statute_name: Notice of Risk to Personal Data Act

maryland.ag_notification_note: The business must notify the Maryland Office of the Attorney General before it notifies affected consumers, with no minimum number of affected residents. The AG notice must include the number of Maryland residents affected, a description of the breach, remediation steps, and a sample of the consumer notice.
maryland.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Attorney General, Division of Consumer Protection
maryland.freeze_rights_note: Under federal law you can place a free security freeze on your credit file at each of the three nationwide bureaus (Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion). A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name, and you can lift or remove it for free whenever you need to apply for credit.
maryland.notification_deadline_note: Notice must be given as soon as reasonably practicable, but no later than 45 days after the business discovers or is notified of the breach. The business must first conduct a good-faith, prompt investigation into whether misuse is likely; if it reasonably finds no likelihood of misuse, no notice is required, but it must keep records of that finding for three years.
maryland.private_right_note: The Personal Information Protection Act creates no direct private lawsuit, but a violation is an unfair or deceptive trade practice under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act, under which consumers can sue for damages and attorneys' fees. Consumers may also file a complaint with the Attorney General's Division of Consumer Protection.
maryland.state_note: Maryland is one of the few states where the Attorney General must be told before you are — the company notifies the AG first, then consumers. The breach notice to you must also include the toll-free numbers and websites for the FTC and the Maryland Attorney General.
maryland.statute_cite: Md. Code Ann., Com. Law §§ 14-3501 et seq.

massachusetts.ag_notification_note: The breached company must notify both the Attorney General and the Office of Consumer Affairs and Business Regulation for every breach, with no minimum number of victims. The notice must describe the breach, say how many residents were affected, and list steps taken or planned.
massachusetts.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit reports with each of the three major credit bureaus, and it is free to place, lift, and remove under federal law. Massachusetts requires the breach notice you receive to explain how to request a freeze and to state that there is no charge for it.
massachusetts.notification_deadline_note: The law sets no fixed number of days. The company must notify you, the Attorney General, and the Office of Consumer Affairs and Business Regulation as soon as practicable and without unreasonable delay once it knows of the breach.
massachusetts.private_right_note: Chapter 93H itself is enforced by the Attorney General, but a violation also counts as an unfair or deceptive practice under Chapter 93A, which lets an injured consumer sue. A company cannot make you give up that right to sue in exchange for free credit monitoring.
massachusetts.state_note: Massachusetts has one of the strictest breach laws in the country: companies must maintain a written information security program, and if your Social Security number was exposed they must offer you at least 18 months of free credit monitoring (42 months if the breached company is a credit bureau).

michigan.ag_notification_note: Michigan law does not require the breached company to notify the Attorney General. If more than 1,000 residents are notified, the company must instead notify the nationwide consumer reporting agencies.
michigan.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit reports with each of the three major credit bureaus, and it is free to place, lift, and remove under federal law. A freeze stops new accounts from being opened in your name while it is in place.
michigan.notification_deadline_note: The statute sets no fixed number of days. Notice must go out without unreasonable delay after the breach is discovered, though the company may take time first to figure out the scope of the breach and restore its systems, or to wait if law enforcement asks it to hold off.
michigan.private_right_note: Only the Attorney General or a county prosecuting attorney can bring an action under this law, seeking civil fines of up to $250 per missed notice (capped at $750,000 per breach). The statute itself gives consumers no right to sue the breached company.
michigan.state_note: Michigan has a harm threshold: the company does not have to notify you if it determines the breach is not likely to cause substantial loss, injury, or identity theft. The notice you do receive must describe the breach, the type of information taken, and give a phone number for help.

minnesota.ag_notification_note: Minnesota law does not require the breached company to notify the Attorney General. The Attorney General appears only as the enforcer of the law. If more than 500 people must be notified at once, the company must notify the nationwide consumer reporting agencies within 48 hours.
minnesota.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit reports with each of the three major credit bureaus, and it is free to place, lift, and remove under federal law. A freeze is the strongest step you can take yourself, since it blocks new accounts from being opened in your name.
minnesota.notification_deadline_note: The statute sets no fixed number of days for telling you. Notice must be made in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay after discovery, allowing time to determine the scope of the breach and to restore the system, or to wait if law enforcement asks for a delay to a specific date.
minnesota.private_right_note: The statute says the Attorney General shall enforce it, and it gives consumers no direct right to sue the breached company for failing to notify them.
minnesota.state_note: Minnesota has an unusually fast 48-hour clock for the credit bureaus: when a breach affects more than 500 people at one time, the company must tell the nationwide consumer reporting agencies within 48 hours, even though there is no fixed deadline for telling you.
minnesota.statute_name: Data Warehouses; Notice Required for Certain Disclosures

mississippi.ag_notification_note: Mississippi law does not require the breached company to notify the Attorney General. Bills proposing an Attorney General notice for breaches affecting 100 or more people were introduced but did not become law.
mississippi.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit reports with each of the three major credit bureaus, and it is free to place, lift, and remove under federal law. You can also check your free credit reports regularly for accounts you did not open.
mississippi.notification_deadline_note: The statute sets no fixed number of days. The company must disclose the breach to all affected individuals without unreasonable delay, after finishing an investigation to determine the nature and scope of the incident and identify who was affected. Law enforcement can ask for a reasonable delay if notice would impede a criminal investigation.
mississippi.private_right_note: The statute says so in plain terms: a failure to comply is an unfair trade practice enforced by the Attorney General, and nothing in the section may be construed to create a private right of action.
mississippi.state_note: Mississippi has a harm threshold: if the company investigates and reasonably determines the breach will not likely result in harm to you, it does not have to notify you at all. If you learn of a breach secondhand, complain to the Attorney General, since only that office can enforce the law.

missouri.ag_notification_note: The company must notify the Attorney General only when it gives notice to more than 1,000 consumers at one time, and then it must tell the Attorney General the timing, distribution, and content of the consumer notice. Smaller breaches require no Attorney General notice.
missouri.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit reports with each of the three major credit bureaus, and it is free to place, lift, and remove under federal law. The breach notice itself must include contact information for the credit bureaus and advice to watch your account statements and free credit reports.
missouri.notification_deadline_note: The statute sets no fixed number of days for telling you. Notice must be made without unreasonable delay after discovery, allowing time to determine the scope of the breach, find contact information, and restore the system, or to wait if law enforcement asks in writing. There is no duty to notify at all if the company determines identity theft or fraud is not reasonably likely and documents that finding in writing.
missouri.private_right_note: The Attorney General has exclusive authority to bring an action under this law, seeking actual damages for a willful and knowing violation and a civil penalty of up to $150,000 per breach. Consumers cannot sue the breached company directly under this statute.
missouri.state_note: Missouri's law covers more kinds of data than most states, including medical information and health insurance information. If you are one of more than 1,000 people notified, the Attorney General gets a copy of the notice, so a complaint to that office is on solid ground.
missouri.statute_name: Notice to Consumer for Breach of Security

montana.ag_notification_note: For every breach in which Montana residents are notified, the company must simultaneously send an electronic copy of the consumer notice, plus a statement of the date and method of distribution, to the Attorney General's Office of Consumer Protection. There is no minimum number of victims.
montana.agency_name: Montana Attorney General, Office of Consumer Protection
montana.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit reports with each of the three major credit bureaus, and it is free to place, lift, and remove under federal law. If the breach notice suggests you get a copy of your credit file, the company must first coordinate the timing and content of that notice with the credit bureau.
montana.notification_deadline_note: The statute sets no fixed number of days. Disclosure must be made without unreasonable delay after discovery, allowing time to determine the scope of the breach and restore the system, or to wait if law enforcement determines notice would impede a criminal investigation.
montana.private_right_note: The breach-notification section itself does not create a private right to sue, but a violation counts as an unfair or deceptive act under Montana's Consumer Protection Act, which does let an injured consumer sue, with treble damages and attorney's fees possible in some cases.
montana.state_note: Montana is unusual in two ways: the Attorney General gets a copy of the notice for every breach, not just big ones, and medical record information counts as personal information that triggers notice. Some secondary roundups wrongly list a 30- or 45-day deadline, but the statute itself says only without unreasonable delay.

nebraska.ag_notification_note: Whenever the company must notify Nebraska residents, it must also notify the Attorney General, no later than the time it notifies residents. There is no minimum number of victims.
nebraska.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit reports with each of the three major credit bureaus, and it is free to place, lift, and remove under federal law. A freeze blocks new credit accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it.
nebraska.notification_deadline_note: The statute sets no fixed number of days. After a good-faith, reasonable, and prompt investigation finds that misuse of your information has occurred or is reasonably likely, the company must notify you as soon as possible and without unreasonable delay, allowing time to determine the scope and restore the system, or to wait if law enforcement asks.
nebraska.private_right_note: Only the Attorney General enforces this law, including the power to seek direct economic damages for each affected resident. The statute gives consumers no private right to sue the breached company.
nebraska.state_note: Nebraska's law covers more than most: a username or email address plus a password that would let someone into an online account counts as personal information, as does unique biometric data such as a fingerprint. The company must investigate first, and only notify if misuse has happened or is reasonably likely.
nebraska.statute_name: Financial Data Protection and Consumer Notification of Data Security Breach Act of 2006

nevada.ag_notification_note: Nevada's breach-notification statute does not require the breached company to notify the Attorney General. If more than 1,000 people must be notified at one time, the company must instead notify the nationwide consumer reporting agencies.
nevada.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit reports with each of the three major credit bureaus, and it is free to place, lift, and remove under federal law. A freeze is the strongest do-it-yourself step after a breach, since it stops new accounts from being opened in your name.
nevada.notification_deadline_note: The statute sets no fixed number of days. Notice must be given in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay after discovery, allowing time to determine the scope of the breach and restore the system, or to wait if law enforcement determines notice would impede a criminal investigation.
nevada.private_right_note: A violation is a deceptive trade practice enforced by the Attorney General, who may seek an injunction. The statute gives consumers no private right to sue; the only civil action it creates lets the breached company sue the person who stole the data.
nevada.state_note: Nevada requires notice only when the breach materially compromises the security, confidentiality, or integrity of your personal information, so a minor exposure may not trigger a notice at all. Some secondary roundups wrongly list 30- or 60-day deadlines, but the statute itself sets no fixed number of days.
nevada.statute_name: Security and Privacy of Personal Information

new hampshire.ag_notification_note: Every breached company must report to the Attorney General, unless it is regulated by another agency with primary authority over its trade, in which case it reports to that regulator instead. The report must include the anticipated date of the consumer notice and the approximate number of people in the state who will be notified.
new hampshire.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit reports with each of the three major credit bureaus, and it is free to place, lift, and remove under federal law. A freeze stops new credit accounts from being opened in your name while it is in place.
new hampshire.notification_deadline_note: The statute sets no fixed number of days. Once the company determines that misuse of your information has occurred, is reasonably likely, or cannot be ruled out, it must notify you as soon as possible and as quickly as possible. Notice may be delayed only if law enforcement or homeland security determines it would impede a criminal investigation.
new hampshire.private_right_note: The breach law itself is enforced by the Attorney General, but a violation counts as an unfair or deceptive act under the Consumer Protection Act (RSA 358-A), which lets an injured consumer sue for damages and attorney's fees.
new hampshire.state_note: New Hampshire uses a misuse test, not just an exposure test: the company must promptly decide how likely it is that your information has been or will be misused, and must notify you if misuse happened, is reasonably likely, or simply cannot be ruled out. If more than 1,000 consumers are notified, the nationwide credit bureaus must be told too.

new jersey.ag_notification_note: New Jersey does not require notice to the Attorney General. Instead, the breached company must report the breach to the Division of State Police in the Department of Law and Public Safety in advance of telling customers. If more than 1,000 people are notified, the nationwide consumer reporting agencies must also be told.
new jersey.agency_name: New Jersey Office of the Attorney General
new jersey.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit reports with each of the three major credit bureaus, and it is free to place, lift, and remove under federal law. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it.
new jersey.notification_deadline_note: The statute sets no fixed number of days for telling you. Disclosure must be made in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay after discovery, allowing time to determine the scope of the breach and restore the system, or to wait if law enforcement asks for a delay. No notice is required if the company establishes that misuse of the information is not reasonably possible.
new jersey.private_right_note: A willful, knowing, or reckless violation is an unlawful practice under the Consumer Fraud Act, and a person who suffers an ascertainable loss of money or property from it may sue for damages. Ordinary or accidental violations do not carry that private right.
new jersey.state_note: New Jersey is the only state in this batch that routes breach reports to the State Police instead of the Attorney General, and the report must go in before customers are told. A breach involving only a username and password has its own rule: the company may simply direct you to promptly change your password and security questions.
new jersey.statute_name: Disclosure of Breach of Security to Customers

new mexico.ag_notification_note: The Attorney General must be notified only if more than 1,000 New Mexico residents must be notified from a single breach, within the same 45 days. Smaller breaches do not trigger AG notice.
new mexico.agency_name: New Mexico Office of the Attorney General
new mexico.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file with each of the three major credit bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it, and it is free to place, lift and remove under federal law.
new mexico.notification_deadline_note: Notice must be given in the most expedient time possible, but no later than 45 calendar days after discovery of the breach. The clock can be paused for a law enforcement request or while the company determines the scope of the breach and restores its system.
new mexico.private_right_note: There is no private right of action under the Data Breach Notification Act. Only the Attorney General may enforce it and seek civil penalties.
new mexico.state_note: New Mexico's law does not apply to the state government or its political subdivisions, and notice is only required for unencrypted personal identifying information reasonably believed to have been subject to a breach.

new york.ag_notification_note: The company must notify the Attorney General, the Department of State and the State Police whenever any New York residents are notified, with no minimum number of people affected. Credit reporting agencies must also be told if more than 5,000 residents are notified at one time.
new york.agency_name: New York State Office of the Attorney General
new york.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file with each of the three major credit bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it, and it is free to place, lift and remove under federal law.
new york.notification_deadline_note: Since the December 2024 amendment, notice must be given in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, and in no event later than 30 days after discovery. The old flexibility to delay while investigating the scope of the breach was removed; only a legitimate law enforcement need can delay notice.
new york.private_right_note: There is no private right of action under the breach notification law or the SHIELD Act. Only the Attorney General may enforce them, although a court in an AG action may award an affected person actual costs or losses.
new york.state_note: New York is unusually broad: mere unauthorized access, not just actual acquisition, can trigger notice, and private information now includes biometric data, online account credentials, and medical and health insurance information. The SHIELD Act also requires businesses to maintain reasonable safeguards, not just to give notice after a breach.
new york.statute_name: SHIELD Act (Stop Hacks and Improve Electronic Data Security Act)

north carolina.ag_notification_note: Whenever a business notifies any affected person, it must also notify the Consumer Protection Division of the Attorney General's Office without unreasonable delay, describing the breach, the number affected and the steps taken. If more than 1,000 people are notified at one time, the credit reporting agencies must also be told.
north carolina.agency_name: North Carolina Attorney General, Consumer Protection Division
north carolina.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file with each of the three major credit bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it, and it is free to place, lift and remove under federal law.
north carolina.notification_deadline_note: The statute sets no fixed number of days. Notice must be given without unreasonable delay after discovery, allowing time to find contact information, determine the scope of the breach and restore the system, and a law enforcement request can delay it.
north carolina.private_right_note: A violation is a violation of the unfair and deceptive trade practices law, but no private suit may be brought unless the individual was injured as a result of the violation.
north carolina.state_note: North Carolina is one of the few states that requires AG notice for any breach, not just a large one, and the breach notice you receive must itself list contact information for the Federal Trade Commission and the Attorney General's Office.

north dakota.ag_notification_note: The Attorney General must be notified by mail or email only if a breach exceeds 250 individuals. Smaller breaches do not trigger AG notice.
north dakota.agency_name: North Dakota Office of Attorney General
north dakota.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file with each of the three major credit bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it, and it is free to place, lift and remove under federal law.
north dakota.notification_deadline_note: The statute sets no fixed number of days. Notice must be given in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, allowing time for law enforcement needs and for steps to determine the scope of the breach and restore the system.
north dakota.private_right_note: The breach notification law provides no private right of action. Enforcement is by the Attorney General under the state's unlawful practices law.
north dakota.state_note: North Dakota's AG threshold is low at 250 people, so many mid-size breaches still reach the Attorney General, and a person who only stores data it does not own must tell the data owner immediately after discovery.
north dakota.statute_name: Notice of Security Breach for Personal Information

ohio.ag_notification_note: The statute does not require notice to the Attorney General. It does require notice to the nationwide consumer reporting agencies, without unreasonable delay, if more than 1,000 Ohio residents are notified in a single occurrence.
ohio.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file with each of the three major credit bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it, and it is free to place, lift and remove under federal law.
ohio.legal_aid_name: Legal Aid of Southeast and Central Ohio
ohio.notification_deadline_note: Notice must be given in the most expedient time possible, but no later than 45 days after discovery or notification of the breach. Notice is only required when the access and acquisition causes, or reasonably is believed will cause, a material risk of identity theft or other fraud.
ohio.private_right_note: There is no private right of action under the breach notification statute. The Attorney General may investigate and bring a civil action for a failure to comply.
ohio.state_note: Ohio is unusual in having no AG-notice duty at all under this statute, so if you were affected, your complaint route is the Attorney General's consumer protection office even though the company was not required to tell that office about the breach.

oklahoma.ag_notification_note: Since January 1, 2026, if 500 or more Oklahoma residents are notified from a single breach, the company must also notify the Attorney General without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after notifying the affected residents. Breaches affecting fewer than 500 residents do not trigger AG notice.
oklahoma.agency_name: Oklahoma Office of the Attorney General
oklahoma.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file with each of the three major credit bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it, and it is free to place, lift and remove under federal law.
oklahoma.notification_deadline_note: The statute sets no fixed number of days for telling affected residents. Notice must be given without unreasonable delay, allowing time to determine the scope of the breach and restore the system, and a law enforcement request can delay it.
oklahoma.private_right_note: The breach notification statute provides no private right of action. A violation that results in injury or loss may be enforced by the Attorney General or a district attorney as an unlawful practice under the Oklahoma Consumer Protection Act.
oklahoma.state_note: Oklahoma's AG-notice duty is new, effective January 1, 2026, and it runs on a different clock from consumer notice: up to 60 days after residents are told. The 2026 amendments also broadened covered data to include biometric data and unique electronic identifiers.

oregon.ag_notification_note: The Attorney General must be notified, in writing or electronically, if more than 250 consumers must be notified, and must receive a copy of any consumer notice within a reasonable time if the breach affects more than 250 consumers.
oregon.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file with each of the three major credit bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it, and it is free to place, lift and remove under federal law. Oregon's breach notice must itself tell you about the credit bureaus and advise you to report suspected identity theft to law enforcement, the Attorney General and the Federal Trade Commission.
oregon.notification_deadline_note: Notice must be given in the most expeditious manner possible, without unreasonable delay, but no later than 45 days after discovering or receiving notification of the breach. A vendor must tell the company it serves within 10 days, and notice can be delayed only on a written law enforcement request.
oregon.private_right_note: A violation is an unlawful practice under the state's unlawful trade practices law, enforced by the Attorney General. The breach notification law itself gives consumers no private right of action, although the statute says other rights and remedies under law are preserved.
oregon.state_note: Oregon requires no consumer notice at all if, after investigation or consultation with law enforcement, the company reasonably determines consumers are unlikely to suffer harm, but it must document that determination in writing and keep it for at least five years.

pennsylvania.ag_notification_note: The Office of Attorney General must be notified concurrently with affected residents if more than 500 Pennsylvania residents must be notified. State agencies must also notify the Attorney General concurrently, even for smaller breaches.
pennsylvania.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file with each of the three major credit bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it, and it is free to place, lift and remove under federal law.
pennsylvania.notification_deadline_note: For a private company, the statute sets no fixed number of days: notice must be given without unreasonable delay after the breach is determined, allowing time to determine the scope and restore the system. State agencies, counties, public schools and municipalities have a tighter 7-business-day deadline.
pennsylvania.private_right_note: The breach notification act itself creates no private right of action. Violations are treated as unfair or deceptive acts enforced by the Attorney General, although consumers may still pursue other theories such as negligence or consumer protection claims.
pennsylvania.state_note: Pennsylvania is one of the few states in this set that requires free credit monitoring: when a breach exposes a Social Security, driver's license, state ID or bank account number, the company must pay for one independent credit report and 12 months of credit monitoring for affected people.
pennsylvania.statute_name: Breach of Personal Information Notification Act

rhode island.ag_notification_note: The Attorney General and the major credit reporting agencies must be notified if more than 500 Rhode Island residents are to be notified, without delaying notice to the affected residents themselves.
rhode island.agency_name: Rhode Island Office of the Attorney General
rhode island.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file with each of the three major credit bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it, and it is free to place, lift and remove under federal law. Rhode Island's breach notice must itself explain how to request a security freeze.
rhode island.notification_deadline_note: For a private company, notice must be given in the most expedient time possible, but no later than 45 calendar days after confirmation of the breach and being able to ascertain the information the notice must contain. State and municipal agencies have 30 calendar days. Notice is only required for a breach that poses a significant risk of identity theft.
rhode island.private_right_note: The Identity Theft Protection Act provides no express private right of action for consumers. A failure to notify is a violation enforced under the act's penalty provisions.
rhode island.state_note: Rhode Island's clock starts at confirmation of the breach, not discovery, and state and municipal agencies must provide remediation services, including at least five years of coverage for adults, while a private company's notice must describe any remediation services it is offering.
rhode island.credit_monitoring_note: Rhode Island requires state and municipal agencies — not private companies — to provide remediation services: at least 5 years of coverage for adults, and coverage until age 18 plus at least 2 more years for minors. A private company's breach notice must describe any remediation services it offers. R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-49.3-4(d)(5), (e).

south carolina.ag_notification_note: Notice goes to the Consumer Protection Division of the Department of Consumer Affairs, not the Attorney General, and only if more than 1,000 South Carolina residents are notified at one time. The nationwide credit reporting agencies must be told at the same threshold.
south carolina.agency_name: South Carolina Department of Consumer Affairs, Consumer Protection Division
south carolina.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file with each of the three major credit bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it, and it is free to place, lift and remove under federal law.
south carolina.notification_deadline_note: The statute sets no fixed number of days. Notice must be given in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay after discovery, allowing time for law enforcement needs and for steps to determine the scope and restore the system. Notice is only required when illegal use has occurred or is reasonably likely, or the use creates a material risk of harm.
south carolina.private_right_note: An injured South Carolina resident may sue: damages for a willful and knowing violation, actual damages only for a negligent violation, plus an injunction and attorney's fees and court costs if successful.
south carolina.state_note: South Carolina routes breach complaints through the Department of Consumer Affairs, which also sets the administrative fine for knowing and willful violations, rather than through the Attorney General, and it is one of the few states in this set where an injured consumer can sue directly under the breach law itself.
south carolina.statute_name: Financial Identity Fraud and Identity Theft Protection Act

south dakota.ag_notification_note: The company must tell the Attorney General only if the breach affects more than 250 South Dakota residents. It must also tell the nationwide credit bureaus whenever it notifies residents.
south dakota.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — federal law makes freezes free, and you must place one separately at each bureau. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it.
south dakota.notification_deadline_note: The company must tell you no later than 60 days after it discovers the breach or is told about it. Notice can be delayed if law enforcement needs it held back, and then it must go out within 30 days after law enforcement says it is okay. No notice is owed at all if the company investigates, tells the Attorney General, and reasonably finds the breach is not likely to harm you.
south dakota.private_right_note: You cannot sue under this law yourself. Only the Attorney General can enforce it, as a deceptive act, with civil penalties of up to $10,000 per day per violation.
south dakota.state_note: South Dakota is one of the few states with a harm test: if the company investigates and reasonably decides the breach will not likely harm you, it can skip telling you — but it still has to tell the Attorney General and keep its written reasoning for three years.

tennessee.ag_notification_note: Tennessee law does not require the company to notify the Attorney General at all. If more than 1,000 people are notified at once, the company must tell the nationwide credit bureaus instead.
tennessee.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — federal law makes freezes free, and you must place one separately at each bureau. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it.
tennessee.legal_aid_name: Legal Aid Society of Middle Tennessee and the Cumberlands
tennessee.notification_deadline_note: The company must tell you no later than 45 days after it discovers the breach or is told about it. Notice can be delayed if law enforcement says it would impede a criminal investigation, and then it must go out within 45 days after law enforcement clears it.
tennessee.private_right_note: Yes. Under Tenn. Code Ann. § 47-18-2107(h), any injured customer (other than a state agency) may sue the company for damages and ask a court to order it to stop violating the law.
tennessee.state_note: Tennessee is unusual in two ways: the company never has to tell the Attorney General, but you can sue the company directly for damages if it breaks this law — most states give you no such right.

texas.ag_notification_note: The company must notify the Attorney General only if the breach involves at least 250 Texas residents. Since September 1, 2023 (SB 768), that AG notice is due as soon as practicable and within 30 days — faster than the 60-day deadline for telling you — and must be filed electronically through the AG's website.
texas.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — federal law makes freezes free, and you must place one separately at each bureau. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it.
texas.notification_deadline_note: The company must tell you without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after the date it determines the breach occurred. It may take extra time to figure out the scope of the breach and fix its systems, or if law enforcement asks for a delay.
texas.private_right_note: You cannot sue under this law yourself. Only the Attorney General enforces it, with civil penalties of $2,000 to $50,000 per violation plus up to $100 per person per day for failing to notify (capped at $250,000 per breach).
texas.state_note: Texas posts breach reports publicly: the Attorney General must publish a listing of the breach notifications it receives on its website, so you can check whether a breach affecting you was reported.
texas.statute_name: Identity Theft Enforcement and Protection Act

utah.ag_notification_note: The company must notify the Office of the Attorney General and the Utah Cyber Center only if the breach involves misuse affecting 500 or more Utah residents. If 1,000 or more residents are affected, it must also tell the nationwide credit bureaus.
utah.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — federal law makes freezes free, and you must place one separately at each bureau. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it.
utah.notification_deadline_note: Utah sets no fixed number of days. Once the company's investigation finds that misuse of your information has happened or is reasonably likely, it must tell you in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, allowing time to determine the scope of the breach and restore its systems.
utah.private_right_note: No. Utah Code § 13-44-301 expressly says the law creates no private right of action. Only the Attorney General enforces it, with penalties up to $2,500 per consumer and $100,000 in total — though claims you already have under other laws, like contract or tort, are preserved.
utah.state_note: Utah has a harm test: the company must first investigate in good faith, and it only has to notify you if that investigation finds misuse has happened or is reasonably likely — a breach alone, with no likely misuse, triggers no notice to you.

vermont.ag_notification_note: Yes, for every breach. The company must give the Attorney General (or the Department of Financial Regulation, for businesses that agency regulates) a preliminary notice within 14 business days of discovery or of notifying consumers, whichever comes first, and must send the AG a copy of the consumer notice.
vermont.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — federal law makes freezes free, and you must place one separately at each bureau. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it. Vermont's own freeze law also makes freezes free.
vermont.notification_deadline_note: The company must tell you in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, but no later than 45 days after it discovers the breach or is told about it. Notice can be delayed at law enforcement's request while an investigation is underway.
vermont.private_right_note: No. The Attorney General and the State's Attorney have sole authority to investigate and enforce the law. A violation is treated as a Consumer Protection Act violation, with penalties up to $10,000 per violation.
vermont.state_note: Vermont has the fastest regulator clock in this group: the company must give the Attorney General a preliminary heads-up within 14 business days, well before the 45-day deadline for telling you — and the AG posts consumer breach notices on its website.

virginia.ag_notification_note: Yes, for every breach — the Attorney General must be told whenever any Virginia resident is notified, with no minimum number of people. If more than 1,000 people are notified at once, the company must also tell the nationwide credit bureaus.
virginia.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — federal law makes freezes free, and you must place one separately at each bureau. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it.
virginia.notification_deadline_note: Virginia sets no fixed number of days. The company must tell you and the Attorney General without unreasonable delay after discovering the breach. It may take reasonable time to determine the scope and fix its systems, or delay if law enforcement says notice would impede an investigation.
virginia.private_right_note: Limited. There is no general right to sue under this law, but the statute preserves your ability to recover direct economic damages caused by a violation. The Attorney General enforces the law and can impose a civil penalty up to $150,000 per breach.
virginia.state_note: Virginia's law sits in the criminal code, not the business code, and its definition of personal information is broader than most: passport numbers and military identification numbers count, along with Social Security and driver's license numbers.

washington.ag_notification_note: The company must notify the Attorney General only if the breach affects more than 500 Washington residents in a single breach, and that notice is also due within 30 days of discovery. State agencies get up to 14 extra days to translate notices.
washington.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — federal law makes freezes free, and you must place one separately at each bureau. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it.
washington.notification_deadline_note: The company must tell you in the most expedient time possible and within 30 days after the breach was discovered — one of the strictest deadlines in the country. It can only delay for law enforcement needs or for the time needed to determine the scope of the breach and restore its systems. No notice is required if the breach is not reasonably likely to put you at risk of harm.
washington.private_right_note: Yes. Under RCW 19.255.040, any consumer injured by a violation may sue for damages, and a violator may also be enjoined. The Attorney General may sue on behalf of the state as well, but AG actions under this chapter cannot be brought under the Consumer Protection Act's private-suit provision.
washington.state_note: Washington is the strictest state in this group: a 30-day deadline, plain-language notices that must say what data was taken, AG notice at 500 people, and a direct right for you to sue for damages — plus a separate breach law (RCW 42.56.590) that covers state and local agencies.
washington.statute_name: Personal Information — Notice of Security Breaches

west virginia.ag_notification_note: West Virginia law requires no notice to the Attorney General. If more than 1,000 people are notified at once, the company must tell the nationwide credit bureaus instead.
west virginia.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — federal law makes freezes free, and you must place one separately at each bureau. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it.
west virginia.notification_deadline_note: West Virginia sets no fixed number of days. The company must tell you without unreasonable delay after discovering the breach, allowing time to determine the scope and restore its systems, or if law enforcement asks for a delay. Notice is only owed if unencrypted, unredacted information was taken and identity theft or fraud has happened or is likely.
west virginia.private_right_note: No. Only the Attorney General enforces the law, and civil penalties apply only for repeated and willful violations, capped at $150,000 per breach or series of breaches.
west virginia.state_note: West Virginia is light on deadlines and regulator notice: no fixed day count, no AG notice, and no notice at all unless the stolen data was unencrypted and identity theft or fraud is caused or likely — but the breach letter itself must tell you about fraud alerts and security freezes.
west virginia.statute_name: Breach of Security of Consumer Information

wisconsin.ag_notification_note: Wisconsin law requires no notice to the Attorney General or any regulator. If 1,000 or more people must be notified in a single incident, the company must tell the nationwide credit bureaus instead.
wisconsin.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — federal law makes freezes free, and you must place one separately at each bureau. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it. Wisconsin's consumer protection agency for identity theft complaints is the Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection (DATCP).
wisconsin.notification_deadline_note: The company must tell you within a reasonable time, and no later than 45 days after it learns your personal information was acquired. What counts as reasonable takes into account how many notices it must send and how it can reach people. Law enforcement can ask the company to hold notice to protect an investigation.
wisconsin.private_right_note: No. The statute creates no private right of action (Fox v. Iowa Health System). Failing to notify you is not negligence by itself, but it can be used as evidence of negligence in a lawsuit under other law. The Attorney General enforces the law.
wisconsin.state_note: Wisconsin's notice duty has a no-risk escape hatch: no notice is owed if the acquisition creates no material risk of identity theft or fraud — and if you do get a notice, you can write to the company and demand it tell you exactly which of your information was acquired.
wisconsin.statute_name: Notice of Unauthorized Acquisition of Personal Information

wyoming.ag_notification_note: Wyoming law requires no notice to the Attorney General or any other regulator. There is no regulator-notice provision in the statute at all.
wyoming.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — federal law makes freezes free, and you must place one separately at each bureau. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it.
wyoming.notification_deadline_note: Wyoming sets no fixed number of days. After the company investigates and finds that misuse of your information has happened or is reasonably likely, it must tell you as soon as possible, in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, allowing for law enforcement needs and for scoping the breach and restoring its systems.
wyoming.private_right_note: No. Only the Attorney General may bring an action to enforce the law and recover damages or other relief. You cannot sue under this statute yourself.
wyoming.state_note: Wyoming is one of the most consumer-unfriendly setups in this group for timing: no day count, no regulator notice, and the company only has to tell you after its own investigation concludes misuse happened or is likely — so if you hear about a breach secondhand, ask the company directly what it found.
wyoming.statute_name: Computer Security Breach; Notice to Affected Persons
